sources.title: Human History Map imported civilization summaries
sources.note: The pre-existing modern demographic summary that counts present-day Dravidian-language speakers and names current ethnolinguistic groups, making it unsuitable for the prehistoric interval.

sources.title: Human History Map 4000 BCE borders

sources.title: Human History Map 3000 BCE borders

sources.title: Human History Map 2000 BCE borders
sources.note: Decoded one-ring southern peninsular polygon, forty-nine positions, bounds, checksum and tested point ownership for 2000 to 1500 BCE.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 BCE borders

sources.title: Human History Map 1000 BCE borders

sources.title: Human History Map 700 BCE borders

sources.title: Human History Map 500 BCE borders
sources.note: Confirmed disappearance of the exact id at its indexed endpoint and documented the many other atlas owners at tested locations.

sources.title: A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Dravidian language family
sources.note: First-hand lexical data recover four major branches and a modelled median family age around 4000 to 4500 years, with broad uncertainty and unresolved homeland and higher branching.

sources.title: The Dravidian Languages: sample chapter
sources.note: Comparative linguistic synthesis defining Dravidian as a language family and distinguishing reconstructed Proto-Dravidian from historically attested daughter languages.

sources.title: A test of Generalized Bayesian dating: A new linguistic dating method
sources.note: Methodological test showing how calibration choices, including Old Tamil attestations, influence statistical dates for a reconstructed language family.

sources.title: Language contact and convergence in South Asia
sources.note: Scholarly account of long South Asian language contact, borrowing and structural convergence, which prevent simple one-language-per-artifact mapping.

sources.title: Dravidian and the Decipherment of the Indus Script
sources.note: Critical review explaining that the Indus inscriptions are short, lack a bilingual, remain undeciphered and do not identify their underlying language.

sources.title: The Formation of Human Populations in South and Central Asia
sources.note: Large ancient-DNA study models changing ancestry clines and population mixture while presenting alternative, explicitly uncertain scenarios for early Dravidian dispersal.

sources.title: Where did the Indus Valley people come from?
sources.note: Nature India account of the single successfully sequenced Rakhigarhi individual, difficult tropical DNA preservation and the limits of one genome for population history.

sources.title: Genetic evidence for recent population mixture in India
sources.note: Genome-wide study dates varying episodes of mixture among sampled present-day populations and demonstrates that genetic histories do not divide into timeless racial blocks.

sources.title: The Archaeology of South Asia: Introduction and Definitions
sources.note: Regional archaeological synthesis cautions against colonial culture labels and describes evidence for stone-tool exchange, subsistence and uneven technological transitions.

sources.title: Dating the Neolithic of South India: new radiometric evidence for key economic, social and ritual transformations
sources.note: Radiocarbon and Bayesian sequence for southern Indian ashmounds, villages, crops and the transition toward Iron Age traditions.

sources.title: A refined chronology for the South Indian Neolithic sequence at Sanganakallu to Kupgal
sources.note: Excavated sequence dates ashmound formation, settlement growth, specialized axe production, changing monumentality and later transition at the Sanganakallu to Kupgal complex.

sources.title: Local diversity in settlement, demography and subsistence across the southern Indian Neolithic to Iron Age transition
sources.note: Integrated survey, radiocarbon, plant and animal evidence shows Sanganakallu growth and abandonment differed from neighboring regional trajectories, partly with water access.

sources.title: Sanganakallu to Kupgal Archaeological Research Project
sources.note: University project overview of the multi-site granite hill complex, excavation history, ashmounds, settlements, craft areas and preservation threats.

sources.title: Sanganakallu to Kupgal intensive systematic survey
sources.note: Systematic transects and mapping distinguish permanent and temporary habitation, quarries, tool workshops, rock shelters, rock art, ashmounds and megaliths.

sources.title: Sanganakallu to Kupgal archaeobotanical research
sources.note: Charred seeds document local small millets, mung bean and horsegram; Hallur evidence includes spindle whorls and charred cotton and flax around 1000 to 900 BCE.

sources.title: Sanganakallu to Kupgal rock art research
sources.note: University fieldwork records petroglyphs along a dolerite dyke and ringing rocks, while keeping their exact performance context interpretively cautious.

sources.title: Rock art and rock music: petroglyphs of the South Indian Neolithic
sources.note: Peer-reviewed survey connects cattle imagery, percussion marks and resonant boulders at Kupgal while distinguishing recorded physical acoustics from inferred ancient performance.

sources.title: Signs of Life: Engraved Stone Artefacts from Neolithic South India
sources.note: Study of deliberately engraved stone artifacts explores image-making and identity without treating designs as a deciphered writing system.

sources.title: Social distinctions during the south Indian Neolithic: changing mortuary practices at Maski
sources.note: Radiometrically dated MARP-79 cemetery shows diverse graves, vessels, coffins, metals and commemoration developing incrementally rather than one abrupt invading culture.

sources.title: Burial Practices in the Neolithic Cultures of South India
sources.note: Institutional archaeological synthesis catalogs southern Neolithic adult and child burials, urns, pits and site differences with their excavation contexts.

sources.title: Indian Archaeology: annual excavation reviews
sources.note: Government archaeological reports for Brahmagiri, Sanganakallu, Piklihal, Maski, Tekkalakota, Hallur, Utnur and related southern sites and material finds.

sources.title: Environmental effects on the spread of the Neolithic crop package to South Asia
sources.note: Archaeobotanical synthesis shows an early southern package of local millets and pulses with cattle, sheep and goats, followed unevenly by wheat and barley.

sources.title: Contrasting Patterns in Crop Domestication and Domestication Rates
sources.note: Plant morphology and find contexts support cultivation of mung bean, horsegram and small millets in dry southern savannah settings.

sources.title: The origins and early dispersal of horsegram, a major crop of ancient India
sources.note: Archaeobotanical synthesis traces a hardy multifunctional pulse and explains why domestication and spread require several well-contextualized seed assemblages.

sources.title: Rice agriculture in Iron Age and Early Historic South India
sources.note: Regional compilation separates the dry millet-pulse Neolithic economy from later and uneven rice expansion around and after the atlas endpoint.

sources.title: Crop assemblages in the highlands of Odisha
sources.note: Archaeobotanical and modern comparative work emphasizes ecological and household crop choice and the limited prehistoric sampling available in eastern India.

sources.title: The political economy of iron in Late Prehistoric South India
sources.note: Kadebakele, Brahmagiri and Maski evidence distinguishes rare smelting, wider smithing, tools, construction pieces, weapons, ornaments and possible inequalities.

sources.title: Finding Ashmounds: Identifying Large Buried Anthropogenic Features with ERT
sources.note: Electrical resistance tomography, drone mapping and exposed sections reveal multiple buried burned-dung deposits at Brahmagiri and correct an older excavation oversight.

sources.title: Brahmagiri and Beyond: The Archaeology of the Southern Neolithic
sources.note: Detailed regional review of hilltop settlements, stone-axe workshops, grinding hollows, beads, pottery, herding and the history of archaeological discovery.

sources.title: Beyond culture history at Maski: Land use, settlement and social differences
sources.note: Landscape project replaces simple artifact stages with long-term evidence for land use, settlement, social difference and later political reorganization around Maski.

sources.title: South Indian Chalcolithic archaeological tradition summary
sources.note: Yale research summary collates settlements, wattle-and-daub houses, ceramics, tools, figurines, ornaments and mortuary evidence across named southern sites.

sources.title: Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro
sources.note: UNESCO describes Indus city planning, wells, baths, drains and sewage disposal; this separate named civilization cannot donate its sanitation to an undeciphered umbrella label.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of India epigraphy digitization background
sources.note: Institutional chronology states that the Indus signs remain undeciphered and securely readable Brahmi evidence is much later, especially third-century BCE Ashokan inscriptions.

sources.title: Passage to India? Anuradhapura and the Early Use of the Brahmi Script
sources.note: Stratified Anuradhapura sherds are argued to provide early fourth-century BCE Brahmi, still outside this record and not evidence for one prehistoric Dravidian voice.

sources.title: Emergence of Early Historic Trade in Peninsular India
sources.note: Synthesis begins around the fifth century BCE and later, showing resource networks and writing immediately beyond the card without projecting them backward.

sources.title: Ancient Skeletal Evidence for Leprosy in India, 2000 BCE
sources.note: Palaeopathological study diagnoses one Balathal skeleton through a specific lesion pattern and illustrates both the power and geographic limits of skeletal disease evidence.

sources.title: Southern Neolithic of India
sources.note: Indian academic teaching synthesis reviews site sequences, circular houses, ceramics, tools, burials and the changing interpretation of southern Neolithic archaeology.

sources.title: Maski 1954: A Chalcolithic Site of the Southern Deccan
sources.note: Primary excavation report documents stratigraphy, pottery, structures, burials and graffiti marks without making those marks a readable language.

sources.title: Landscape and Cosmology in the South Indian Neolithic
sources.note: Contextual study asks how ashmounds organized movement, memory and gathering while marking cosmological interpretations as archaeological arguments rather than recovered doctrine.

sources.title: Southern Neolithic cultivation systems: an archaeobotanical reconstruction
sources.note: Site-by-site crop evidence reconstructs dry cultivation, processing and seasonal work without assuming one uniform cuisine or farming calendar.

sources.title: Settlement pattern of the South Indian Ashmound Tradition
sources.note: Regional comparison distinguishes villages rich in grinding evidence from short-stay cattle-penning camps and proposes linked, not identical, farming and herding places.

proposedOverrides.summary: A cautious guide to the many prehistoric South Asian communities placed under the atlas’s “Dravidians” umbrella, keeping language reconstruction, archaeology and genetics separate while exploring southern farming, herding, craft, households, health and change from 4000 to 500 BCE.
